newsitem.title: GERMANY: EUROPEANS TO BLUNT DOLLAR, CALM EMU FEARS AT IMF MEETING.
newsitem.headline: EUROPEANS TO BLUNT DOLLAR, CALM EMU FEARS AT IMF MEETING.

text.p: European financial leaders will use this weekend's World Bank/International Monetary Fund meeting to head off further dollar gains and calm jitters about European monetary union (EMU), economists said on Tuesday.

Analysts said European finance ministers and central bankers, who will meet their counterparts from the G7 group of industrialised nations on the fringes of the IMF meeting, were unlikely to announce any change to existing exchange rate policies.

But they added that the G7 officials -- from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- would also be unable to resist making comments to reporters covering the Spring meeting.

"We are not going to see official pronouncements, but you could see remarks about when to stop the dollar, where to stop it and how to stop it," said Holger Schmieding, senior economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
Although the dollar rate against the yen will take centre stage, officials are likely also to sound off on the dollar/mark.
The dollar, which began April at around 1.66-1.67 marks, rallied steadily to hit a 37-month high of 1.7375 on April 15. It has has recently leveled off to trade near 1.7040.
The stronger U.S. currency has raised fears of "imported inflation" in Europe, where countries must now pay more for goods such as energy which are often priced in dollars.
So far German authorities have expressed satisfaction with the dollar/mark rate, but analysts said they will want to ensure that the U.S. currency does not climb much higher.
"The Bundesbank showed at its press conference last week that it does not want the mark to weaken much futher," said Timo Klein, analyst at MMS International.
Analysts said they expect German authorities to try and verbally stay the dollar's advance, indicating satisfaction with current exchange rate levels in vaguely-worded comments.
"They are likely to say something like, "the dollar/mark now corresponds with fundamentals," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF-Bank .
He and others also expect European officials to offer what are by now routine reassurances that European economic and monetary union (EMU) will start on time on January 1, 1999.
That will mean papering over difficulties that many are having in trimming their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product as is required for EMU members.
"If Waigel (Germany's finance minister) is asked about if Germany will qualify for EMU, he will only beam and say 'no problem'," Klein said.

Some analysts thought there was a good chance that German and French officials could met privately to work on ways to launch EMU without Italy and Spain -- two countries that the Bundesbank is thought to feel lack a "stability culture".
Rumours of such a deal have circulated in financial markets for weeks and have been denied by both Bonn and Paris.
European elections could also alter the meeting's tone.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis will keep voters in mind with President Jacques Chirac on Monday calling a snap election for May 25 and June 1.
The election has reignited political doubts about EMU and Arthuis is likely to use the meeting to restate France's commitment to the project.

Italian officials, meanwhile, will probably defend their own efforts to qualify for EMU. Rome has been criticised for not addressing structural problems which some feel make Italy an unreliable EMU partner.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi has repeatedly said he wants Rome to join the first group of contries to form a single currency and that he will resign if the country fails to make the grade. REUTER
